q: A bridge is on its third extension. What does each repeat do?
a: Escalates approval higher each time — repeat bridges are a planning failure wearing an urgency costume.
d: Nothing — extensions inherit the original approval.
Resets the J&A posting clock.
Converts the bridge into a logical follow-on.
x: Each repeat bridge escalates to higher approval — the system's way of making planning failures expensive. Extensions don't inherit the first approval; every one re-justifies against a bar that keeps rising.

q: Why is apparent authority the trap in UAC cases?
a: Because looking authorized isn't being authorized — the contractor can't rely on it, and neither can you.
d: Because apparent authority binds the Government retroactively.
Because it converts automatically to implied authority.
Because ratification cures it without any investigation.
x: Apparent authority is the trap because it FEELS binding on the ground — a colonel said go — but binds nothing legally. The contractor can't rely on it and neither can you; only ratification by actual authority fixes what it breaks.

q: Name the classic examples of source selection information.
a: Proposed rankings, the source selection plan, evaluation results, competitive-range lists, the Government estimate.
d: The synopsis, the PWS, and the wage determination.
CPARS ratings and SAM registration data.
The clause matrix and Section K representations.
x: The classics: proposed rankings, the source selection plan, evaluation results, competitive-range lists, the Government estimate. If it could hand an offeror an edge in THIS competition, treat it as SSI and control it.

q: When must you spot an OCI to have real options?
a: Early — before solicitation; avoid, neutralize, and mitigate all work best pre-release.
d: At award — that's when the conflict legally attaches.
During discussions, once proposals are in.
At the debrief, when offerors raise it.
x: OCI options exist before solicitation: you can still avoid (change the requirement), neutralize (restructure), or mitigate (firewall). After proposals arrive, most doors have closed and exclusion may be all that's left. Early is everything.

q: Responsibility is decided as of when, on what evidence?
a: At award, on the record before the CO — today's facts, documented.
d: At proposal receipt, on SAM status alone.
At solicitation release, on CPARS history.
Continuously — it's re-decided at each invoice.
x: Responsibility is decided at award, on documented facts as they stand that day — not proposal-time snapshots, not continuous re-adjudication. A firm non-responsible today can be responsible next quarter; the determination is dated for a reason.

q: Bundling rides on which research finding?
a: Whether consolidating the requirement is necessary and justified — the research has to support it.
d: Whether the incumbent can absorb the added work.
Whether two NAICS codes share a size standard.
Whether GSA offers a comparable schedule.
x: Bundling — consolidating requirements small businesses used to win separately — must be necessary and justified, and the market research is where that case lives or dies. It's a research finding, not a convenience call.

q: What makes a source "mandatory" — and what doesn't unlock the open market?
a: Being on the procurement list; price alone doesn't unlock the open market.
d: Agency preference; a D&F unlocks it.
A GSA listing; the ombudsman unlocks it.
Set-aside status; a J&A unlocks it.
x: Mandatory means on the procurement list and meeting the need — and price alone doesn't unlock the open market. Fit and availability problems go through the program channels, documented; unilateral 'it's cheaper commercial' is the violation pattern.

q: Which termination framework rides with commercial contracts?
a: The commercial clause's cause/convenience framework — not Part 49's machinery.
d: Part 49 in full, like any other contract.
T4D with cure notices under 49.x.
No termination rights at all — that's the commercial trade.
x: Commercial contracts terminate under the commercial clause's cause/convenience framework — Part 49's cure-notice machinery and reprocurement remedies don't apply as such. Boards love this seam; knowing which regime you're in is the answer.

q: SAP exists for what two purposes?
a: Speed routine buys with less paperwork, and create small-business opportunity.
d: Avoid competition and reduce protest exposure.
Extend GPC limits and defer funding.
Test vendors before committing to IDIQ awards.
x: SAP exists to speed routine buys with proportionate paperwork AND to create small-business opportunity — the MPT-to-SAT reservation is baked into the band. It's not competition avoidance; it's competition right-sized.

q: HUBZone brings what feature in full-and-open competition?
a: A price evaluation preference.
d: An automatic 10% technical rating bonus.
Exemption from responsibility determinations.
First-refusal rights on the award.
x: In full-and-open competition, HUBZone firms get a price evaluation preference — their offer is evaluated as if competing offers cost more. It's the one program benefit that operates INSIDE unrestricted competition rather than through a set-aside.

q: "We've always used this vendor" is…?
a: Not a reason — habit isn't an exception; the default is competition.
d: A logical follow-on rationale.
Exception (1) in embryo — document it and proceed.
Acceptable below $10M.
x: Incumbency is a fact, not an exception. 'We've always used them' appears nowhere in RFO 6.103 — if the incumbent is genuinely the only capable source, prove THAT with research; the history alone justifies nothing.

q: Cost/price and what else are mandatory evaluation factors?
a: Quality — and confirm the current evaluation rules under RFO Part 15.
d: Past performance and small-business participation, always.
Schedule and data rights.
None — evaluation factors are fully discretionary.
x: Cost/price and quality are the mandatory factors — with the standing caveat to confirm current RFO Part 15 evaluation rules, since the overhaul trimmed the legacy mandates. Past performance is common but no longer the universal mandate people remember.

topic: Certified Cost or Pricing Data & Proposal Analysis
q: Who signs the Certificate of Current Cost or Pricing Data, and when?
a: The contractor, at agreement on price — certifying the data current, accurate, and complete.
d: The CO, at award.
DCAA, after the post-agreement sweep.
The contractor's counsel, at proposal submission.
x: The contractor signs the Certificate of Current Cost or Pricing Data at price agreement — certifying the data was current, accurate, and complete AS OF that agreement. That certificate is what makes defective pricing enforceable later.

q: Why does CPIF need a "credible target"?
a: The incentive only disciplines cost if the target means something — a fantasy target pays fee for noise.
d: Because DCAA audits the target annually.
It doesn't — CPIF works at any target.
Because fee is capped at 10% of target cost.
x: CPIF's fee swing only disciplines cost if the target is credible — a fantasy target pays fee for noise, punishing or rewarding luck. No believable target, no incentive contract: that honesty check is the type-selection discipline.

q: Fair opportunity means every holder gets what?
a: A real chance to be considered for each order — genuine consideration, not rotation paperwork.
d: An equal share of orders over the vehicle's life.
A guaranteed minimum on each order.
A debrief on every order, at any value.
x: Fair opportunity means each holder gets genuinely considered for each order — real evaluation, not rotation paperwork or 'considered but lost' templates. If your record couldn't convince the ombudsman the consideration was real, it wasn't.

q: Options are evaluated when, and priced when?
a: Both at award — that's exactly what makes later exercise unilateral.
d: Both at exercise.
Priced at award, evaluated at exercise.
Evaluated at award, repriced at exercise.
x: Options are evaluated AND priced at award — that's what earns the Government the unilateral right to exercise later. An option that was never evaluated or priced can't simply be exercised; it's a new negotiation wearing an option's clothes.

q: The assisted-acquisition agreement must define what, before funds move?
a: Roles and responsibilities — who does what between the agencies.
d: The protest venue for future orders.
The servicing agency's fee cap.
A NAICS crosswalk between the agencies.
x: Before a dollar moves in an assisted acquisition, the interagency agreement defines roles: who solicits, who awards, who administers, whose rules govern. Money without a role map is how interagency actions end up in GAO reports.

q: Non-severable effort funded incrementally "to stretch the money" — problem?
a: Yes — non-severable work must be fully funded up front; incremental funding there is a fiscal violation.
d: No — increments are always authorized for services.
Only if the effort crosses fiscal years.
Only above the SAT.
x: Non-severable work is a bona fide need of the award year and must be fully funded up front — incremental funding to 'stretch the money' violates Time and Amount at once. Severability isn't a style choice; it's a funding-law classification.

q: Limited rights vs. restricted rights — which attaches to what?
a: Limited → technical data; restricted → computer software (both born of private-expense development).
d: Limited → software; restricted → technical data.
Both attach only to mixed-funding items.
Limited → hardware; restricted → firmware.
x: Limited rights attach to technical data, restricted rights to computer software — both born of private-expense development. Same concept, two vocabularies, and boards check whether you match the right label to the right subject matter.

q: In-scope mods and the synopsis — what's the rule?
a: In-scope mods aren't competed or synopsized; out-of-scope work is new work — compete it or justify it.
d: All mods over $150K are synopsized.
Synopsis is required only for cost growth over 25%.
Out-of-scope mods may proceed on bilateral signature alone.
x: In-scope mods ride the original competition — no synopsis, no new competition. Out-of-scope work is a new procurement: compete it or justify it under Part 6. The synopsis question is answered entirely by the scope analysis.

q: Furnishing GFP changes the Government's posture how?
a: The Government takes on performance obligations — late or faulty GFP is Government-caused delay.
d: It shifts all property risk to the contractor.
It has no schedule significance.
It converts the contract to cost-type.
x: GFP puts the Government ON the performance path: late or defective property is Government-caused delay with equitable-adjustment exposure. You're not just lending equipment — you're accepting schedule obligations.

q: Why do UCAs weaken the Government's negotiating position?
a: The contractor performs while the price is open — comfort without cost pressure; leverage decays monthly.
d: They don't — the NTE ceiling protects the position.
Because clearance happens at award.
Because fee is locked at the UCA stage.
x: Undefinitized performance is cost-reimbursement comfort at negotiation leverage: every month without a definitized price, actuals accumulate and your position decays. The caps and the 180-day clock are the counterweights — enforce them.

q: Clearance protects against what, fundamentally?
a: Committing the Government before an independent set of eyes checks strategy, price, and compliance.
d: Contractor default after award.
ADA violations at obligation.
Debrief disputes before award.
x: Clearance is the independent check between 'we negotiated it' and 'the Government is bound by it' — strategy, price support, and compliance verified by someone who doesn't own the deal. It exists because self-review is no review.

q: The agency-protest venue's superpower?
a: Speed and self-correction — fixing your own error fastest, without GAO.
d: An automatic stay stronger than GAO's.
Binding precedent for future buys.
Recovery of proposal costs.
x: The agency protest is fastest and self-correcting — your own agency fixing its own error without GAO's 100-day process. Its limits: no automatic-stay teeth like GAO, no binding judgment like COFC. Speed is the trade.

q: Interest on a claim runs from when?
a: When the CO receives the certified claim.
d: The date performance costs were incurred.
The CO's final decision.
The notice of appeal.
x: CDA interest runs from the CO's RECEIPT of the certified claim — not from costs incurred, not from the final decision. That start date is why misclassifying a functional claim as an REA is expensive: the meter was already running.

q: T4C exists because the Government reserves what?
a: The right to end a contract in the Government's best interest — with the contractor made whole for work done.
d: The right to re-compete every contract annually.
A price-reduction remedy for market drops.
An offset against the contractor's future awards.
x: T4C is the Government's reserved right to end a contract in its best interest — needs change, programs die — with the contractor made whole for work performed. It's the escape valve that makes long-term Government contracting possible at all.

q: OTs trade away what, for agility?
a: The mature protections framework of regulation-based contracting — spend that trade only when it buys something.
d: Intellectual-property rights entirely.
Access to nontraditional contractors.
Competition requirements — OTs are sole-source by design.
x: OTs trade the mature protections framework — competition rules, cost principles, disputes machinery — for agility. That trade is worth making only when it buys something real: nontraditionals at the table, prototype-speed terms. Never as rule avoidance.

q: A&E selection runs on what basis?
a: Qualifications-based selection, then fair-price negotiation with the most qualified firm.
d: Lowest price among technically acceptable designers.
A best-value tradeoff, like any service.
Rotation among registered local firms.
x: A&E runs on qualifications-based selection: rank firms on qualifications, negotiate price with the most qualified. Design quality drives lifecycle cost far more than design fee — the statute does that math for you.
